implementation_notes: kotlinx.coroutines names the decision in the constructor: Channel(capacity = n, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.SUSPEND or DROP_OLDEST or DROP_LATEST), with Channel.CONFLATED as the shorthand for capacity 1 plus DROP_OLDEST, Channel.RENDEZVOUS as capacity 0, and Channel.UNLIMITED as the (deliberate) removal of the bound. Because send() suspends instead of blocking a thread, the suspend policy costs no OS thread, and the reject policy is trySend(), which returns a result instead of waiting. onUndeliveredElement is the hook that runs for every element the buffer sacrificed, which is how a dropped item's resources (file handles, buffers) still get released; the same capacity/policy pair is available in the Flow.buffer operator when the buffer sits between two pipeline stages.
pitfalls: trySend() failure conflates 'buffer full' and 'channel closed': ChannelResult exposes isClosed/isFailure, and treating shutdown as back-pressure hides a lifecycle bug.
DROP_OLDEST/DROP_LATEST discard elements silently unless onUndeliveredElement is set, which leaks anything the element owned.
A channel delivers each element to exactly one receiver, and closing it aborts the delivery of buffered elements - drain before close when the tail matters.

variants.name: Flow.buffer as a pipeline stage
variants.implementation_notes: In a cold pipeline the same bound is a stage instead of a channel: buffer(capacity = n, onBufferOverflow = ...) inserts an explicitly sized buffer between upstream and downstream, which is the operator the coroutines guides describe as detaching their rates, and it accepts the identical BufferOverflow strategies. Choose it over a hand-made Channel when the queue exists to decouple two operators rather than to hand work to unrelated coroutines, and remember that the operator is backed by a channel internally, so the semantics - suspend, drop oldest, drop latest - are exactly those of the channel constructor. The channel form is still the right one for a shared work queue with several consumers.
variants.code_sketch:
source
  .buffer(capacity = 1_000, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)  // bound + policy
  .map { process(it) }
  .collect()
pitfalls: buffer() applies to the upstream side of the stage: placing it after a slow operator only buffers the output and hides the real bottleneck.
DROP_OLDEST in a flow silently reorders the loss relative to the collector: if the pipeline is order-sensitive, dropping is a correctness decision, not a tuning knob.
An explicit large buffer in a Flow chain makes the pipeline look back-pressure-safe while the queue absorbs the imbalance; keep the size tied to a latency budget.
